title: Three weeks later: what actually survives an extraction in DEEPWELL
author: Verciau
selftext:
Three weeks ago I [shared DEEPWELL here](https://www.reddit.com/r/aigamedev/comments/1wziroj/im_building_an_extraction_deckbuilder_solo_with/), my solo deckbuilding roguelite with extraction risk. The most useful part of that thread was the discussion about whether those two ideas actually belong together.

One comment put the problem clearly: a good deckbuilder lets you build a ridiculous engine, enjoy it, then reset. An extraction game asks you to leave with something worth keeping. Carry too much power forward and the next run can become a formality.

I talked about this in the comments, but wanted to follow up with how the current version handles it. Your collection holds individual card copies. The upgrades and relic combinations that made a particular run powerful reset. You can bring selected copies into your next dive, but those copies are now at risk. The rest of your collection stays home.

What you choose to bring also changes how deep you have to go before you can extract. So choosing a stronger starting loadout comes with a commitment. Get out successfully and you bring your committed cards home along with the eligible cards and rewards you picked up. Die and you lose the copies you brought and the unbanked haul. Permanent unlocks and card appearances stay yours.

There's also a Free Dive, where none of your owned copies are at risk. I want losing a good deck to leave you wanting another attempt, with a way to rebuild. Whether that recovery feels rewarding or becomes a chore is one of the things I still need people to challenge.

On the AI development side, a lot of my recent work has been small, specific fixes: damage previews matching what a card will actually do, enemy intents staying readable, and saves recovering properly. I use agents to trace those problems and work through fixes, with validation harnesses for the rules and repeated checks in the game for how it feels. Getting a convincing answer from an agent is easy. Finding the case it missed takes more work.

That has been the useful distinction for me throughout this project. AI can help me build and check a system, but it can't settle whether losing a favorite card feels exciting, annoying, or simply unfair. Snowballing is still something I want playtesters to push on.

The web build is still a gated playtest; early-access signups are at [playdeepwell.com](https://playdeepwell.com/).

For people who enjoy both genres: what would make you voluntarily extract from a run when your deck is finally working?
